title: How To Get Students To Turn On Their Zoom Camera
author: Michael Linsin
summary: For teachers who cannot mandate cameras-on policies, Linsin argues the most effective lever is not persuasion but the teacher's own on-camera behavior. He recommends three moves: 'share,' meaning teachers openly show their own imperfect, cluttered home office to normalize imperfection for students; 'enjoy,' meaning teachers make a deliberate decision to have fun regardless of circumstances rather than waiting to feel like it; and 'focus,' meaning teachers lean into visible engagement with the students they can see, which naturally draws in others. He explicitly separates this article's URL topic from its actual title, noting the strategy works alongside — not instead of — practical fixes like virtual backgrounds. He closes by acknowledging valid arguments against mandatory cameras but arguing teachers must still find creative, psychological ways to make students want to turn cameras on rather than accepting a wall of blank screens.
points: Show students your own imperfect, cluttered home environment to normalize imperfection and reduce their self-consciousness.
Decide deliberately, before each lesson, to have fun regardless of circumstances rather than waiting to feel like it.
Lean into visible engagement and eye contact with students whose cameras are on to draw in the rest of the class.
Practical fixes like virtual backgrounds and earphones help but work best combined with these behavioral strategies.
Making students want to turn their camera on is more effective long-term than simply mandating or pleading for it.
quotes: It’s to teach and behave in such a way that students want to turn their camera on.
When students see that perfect doesn’t exist, that even their teacher has interruptions and dogs barking in the background, then they’re more likely to join in.
The pressure to be perfect— the evil culture —has infected our profession with a dark seriousness that makes it drudgery.
You must loosen up all on your own and refuse to be a victim of circumstance or the whims of your school district.
It’s okay to smile and laugh and have fun with your students online, as it is in the classroom.
We use the power of reciprocity and belongingness to inspire students to make the right decisions on their own behalf.
